overview: This file traces electric-power problems in Japan and East Asia from the immediate postwar period through 1949. It begins with the Shanghai Power Company’s unsuccessful attempt to obtain generating equipment from Japan as reparations, continues with an academic inquiry into Japanese railway electrification, and contains extensive 1948 reporting on the rehabilitation of Japan’s hydroelectric and thermal plants, labor disputes, coal shortages, and SCAP involvement. A separate despatch documents South Korea’s severe power deficit after North Korea ended deliveries across the 38th parallel, while the final airgram records approval of a major Counterpart Fund loan for new Japanese generating and transmission facilities.

subfiles.title: Robertson request for Japanese generating equipment for Shanghai
subfiles.from: W. S. Robertson, President, American & Foreign Power Company, Inc.
subfiles.to: James F. Byrnes, Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Robertson asks whether steam-electric generating units in Japan can be transferred promptly to the damaged Shanghai Power Company.
subfiles.summary: Robertson asks for Japanese generating units for the war-damaged Shanghai Power Company, anticipating a capacity shortfall within five months, referencing Pauley's plans to remove Japanese equipment.

subfiles.title: State Department rejection of Robertson's equipment request
subfiles.from: Edwin M. Martin, Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: The State Department explains why Japanese generating equipment cannot yet be transferred to the Shanghai Power Company.
subfiles.summary: Martin tells Robertson Japanese equipment is reserved for reparations and unavailable for sale, with no Allied allocation authority yet, promising an announcement when deliveries become possible.

subfiles.title: Federal Power Commission referral of Singleton inquiry
subfiles.from: J. H. Gutride, Acting Secretary, Federal Power Commission
subfiles.about: The Federal Power Commission forwards C. W. Singleton's request for information on Japanese electric-power development and railway electricity use.
subfiles.summary: The Commission explains that it cannot supply the requested foreign-power information and therefore refers Singleton's letter to the State Department. Pages 4 and 5 are marked and clean copies of the same referral, identifying Singleton's letter as enclosure No. 37047.

subfiles.title: Singleton inquiry on Japanese railway electrification
subfiles.from: C. W. Singleton, University of Toledo
subfiles.about: Singleton requests data on Japanese power development and the use of electricity by Japan's railroads.
subfiles.summary: Singleton, researching Japan's railways, asks about electric-power development and railway electrification extent, in a letter later dated to January 1947.

subfiles.title: Federal Power Commission acknowledgment to Singleton
subfiles.from: J. H. Gutride, Acting Secretary, Federal Power Commission
subfiles.about: The Commission tells Singleton that his inquiry has been referred to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: Federal Power Commission tells Singleton it doesn't compile foreign power data and forwards his inquiry to State.

subfiles.title: State Department statistics on Japanese railway power consumption
subfiles.from: Charles L. Hodge, Acting Associate Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Hodge supplies limited prewar statistics on electric-power consumption by Japanese railways.
subfiles.summary: State gives Singleton Japanese railway power-consumption averages: 0.888 billion units (1928-29), 1.141 billion (1930-34), and 1.347 billion (1935-36), promising more data later.

subfiles.title: Internal review of Mizutani memorandum
subfiles.about: An internal State Department memorandum assesses Mizutani's explanation of delays in rehabilitating Japanese power plants.
subfiles.summary: Reviewer finds Mizutani's memo aims to rebut Strike Mission criticism, blame unions for delays, and seek more coal, calling it an attempt to pass blame to labor and lean on SCAP.

subfiles.title: Sebald despatch transmitting Mizutani power-industry memorandum
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, Acting Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Sebald forwards and contextualizes a Japanese Commerce and Industry Ministry memorandum on delayed power-plant rehabilitation.
subfiles.summary: Sebald forwards Mizutani's memo defending against Overseas Consultants' criticism, blaming union strikes and demands for repair delays, proposing joint inspection teams, worker priority provisioning, and more coal for thermal plants.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on problems confronting Japan's electric-power industry
subfiles.from: Chōzaburō Mizutani / Japanese Ministry of Commerce and Industry
subfiles.to: Chief, Economic and Scientific Section, SCAP
subfiles.about: The enclosure details plant rehabilitation, coal requirements, electric-industry labor disputes, and delays at the Yamazato and Inawashiro hydroelectric plants.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum argues that most generating-plant repairs are progressing but that union meetings, localized disputes, work restrictions, and demands for wages and rations are causing significant delays. It seeks joint GHQ–Japanese inspection teams and additional coal, estimating January and February thermal capacity and consumption by district and warning that coal stocks are far below target. An appendix describes the approximately 100,000-member Electric Industry Workers' Union and its “business strike,” then gives detailed output, damage, staffing, and repair information for the flooded Yamazato plant and the Inawashiro First plant, where a 1912 German-made turbine casing burst.
keywords: Japan Power Generation and Transmission Company

subfiles.title: Bunce despatch on electric power in South Korea
subfiles.about: Bunce transmits a South Korean power report and summarizes the American Electric Power Mission's inspections and the consequences of North Korea's power cutoff.
subfiles.summary: Bunce forwards a South Korean power handbook and mission inspection findings; after North Korea cut power May 14, 1948, output fell from 100,000 to 60,000 kilowatts, with winter shortages urging thermal-capacity restoration.

subfiles.title: Airgram announcing Counterpart Fund loan to Nippon Hassoden
subfiles.about: The airgram reproduces a GHQ announcement approving a Counterpart Fund loan for Japanese power-generation and transmission projects.
subfiles.summary: Airgram announces SCAP's 1.834-billion-yen loan to Nippon Hassoden for five hydro and two steam plants and 122 km of transmission lines, the first of several loans to ease Japan's power shortage.

interest: Shows 1945-49 shift from Japanese reparations to American-financed power reconstruction, amid labor disputes and Korean partition power cuts.
